title: Does Organic Mean No Pesticides?
question: Does organic farming really mean no pesticides, and are the ones it uses safer?
alternates: What Organic Farmers Are Allowed to Spray
Organic Pesticides: Fewer, Mostly Milder, Not All Harmless
premise: Organic farming does use pesticides. US rules (7 CFR 205.206) let organic producers apply biological, botanical or National List substances when preventive practices fail, and 7 CFR 205.601 lists synthetic ones among them, such as insecticidal soaps, horticultural oils, lime sulfur and copper fungicides. In the EU, 26 of 385 authorised pesticide substances are also approved for organic farming, plus two synthetic pyrethroids allowed only in insect traps. That list is mostly of low concern: 10 of the 26 have any identified toxicity, against 340 of all 385, and none is classed as a suspected carcinogen or reproductive toxicant (27 and 26 among all approved). The exceptions are real: pyrethrins act like synthetic pyrethroids, and copper is toxic at high intakes and harmful to aquatic life. These are EU hazard classes, not measured exposure or harm, and the US list differs.
whyWatch: Many shoppers pay for organic believing nothing was sprayed. The organic rulebook says otherwise, and the EU's hazard classifications show how the pesticides organic farms may use compare with the rest.
tension: Dozens of videos say organic means pesticide-free; sceptics answer that organic pesticides are no safer than synthetic ones. The rules show organic farms do spray, and the hazard data show the organic list is mostly milder, with two real exceptions.

arc.hook: Ask what the viewer thinks organic farmers spray, then read the rule that says when they may.
arc.conflict: The sources do not agree, and both sides have a case.
arc.evidence: Lay the studies side by side (USDA AMS 2010-2011 pilot, residue testing of retail organic produce, USDA organic regulations (7 CFR 205), Mie 2017 review, health effects of organic food and farming, Baranski 2014 meta-analysis, organic crops): design, sample, what was measured.
arc.resolution: Organic is a short list of pesticides used after prevention, mostly natural and mostly of low concern, with a few synthetic exceptions and two natural ones, pyrethrins and copper, that are not harmless; it is not pesticide-free farming.
arc.takeaway: The conditions under which the claim holds, instead of a yes or no.

central.text: The evidence does not support "Organic farming uses no pesticides"

guess.note: The USDA National List and EU rules permit a set of natural and some synthetic pesticides in organic farming.

questions.question: Does organic farming really mean no pesticides, and are the ones it uses safer?

central.text: The evidence does not support "Organic farming uses no pesticides"

questions.premise: Organic farming does use pesticides. US rules (7 CFR 205.206) let organic producers apply biological, botanical or National List substances when preventive practices fail, and 7 CFR 205.601 lists synthetic ones among them, such as insecticidal soaps, horticultural oils, lime sulfur and copper fungicides. In the EU, 26 of 385 authorised pesticide substances are also approved for organic farming, plus two synthetic pyrethroids allowed only in insect traps. That list is mostly of low concern: 10 of the 26 have any identified toxicity, against 340 of all 385, and none is classed as a suspected carcinogen or reproductive toxicant (27 and 26 among all approved). The exceptions are real: pyrethrins act like synthetic pyrethroids, and copper is toxic at high intakes and harmful to aquatic life. These are EU hazard classes, not measured exposure or harm, and the US list differs.
questions.tension: Dozens of videos say organic means pesticide-free; sceptics answer that organic pesticides are no safer than synthetic ones. The rules show organic farms do spray, and the hazard data show the organic list is mostly milder, with two real exceptions.
questions.whyWatch: Many shoppers pay for organic believing nothing was sprayed. The organic rulebook says otherwise, and the EU's hazard classifications show how the pesticides organic farms may use compare with the rest.

arc.hook: Ask what the viewer thinks organic farmers spray, then read the rule that says when they may.
arc.conflict: The sources do not agree, and both sides have a case.
arc.evidence: Lay the studies side by side (USDA AMS 2010-2011 pilot, residue testing of retail organic produce, USDA organic regulations (7 CFR 205), Mie 2017 review, health effects of organic food and farming, Baranski 2014 meta-analysis, organic crops): design, sample, what was measured.
arc.resolution: Organic is a short list of pesticides used after prevention, mostly natural and mostly of low concern, with a few synthetic exceptions and two natural ones, pyrethrins and copper, that are not harmless; it is not pesticide-free farming.
arc.takeaway: The conditions under which the claim holds, instead of a yes or no.

questions.question: Does eating organic actually lower the pesticides you take in?

central.text: Switching to an organic diet quickly lowers pesticide levels in the body

questions.premise: Yes, by a lot, though not to zero. EU monitoring found quantifiable residues in 43.7% of all samples against 13.8% of organic ones, and a meta-analysis found detectable residues on 46% of conventional and 11% of organic crops, though few studies compared concentrations; US monitoring summarised by Winter and Katz still found residues on 23% of organic samples. Whole-diet switch trials in children and adults cut urinary pesticide metabolites, by up to 90%, within a few days. These are exposure measures; whether the lower exposure improves health is not established here.
questions.tension: Organic produce is sold as residue-free, and sceptics say the difference is trivial. Monitoring finds residues on organic food too, yet people's urinary pesticide levels drop sharply within days of switching.
questions.whyWatch: Lower pesticide exposure is the most common reason people buy organic. Food monitoring and diet-switch trials measure it directly, and the effect is large and fast, while the health payoff is a separate, open question.

arc.hook: Swap a family's food to organic for a week and measure what comes out in their urine.
arc.conflict: The claims pulling in different directions: "Organic produce carries lower pesticide residues than conventional produce"; "Switching to an organic diet quickly lowers pesticide levels in the body"; "Pesticide residues on conventional produce are too low to harm health"; "Organic farming uses no pesticides"; "Pesticides allowed in organic farming are not necessarily safer than synthetic ones"; "The Dirty Dozen list is a reliable guide to which produce to buy organic"; "Washing produce removes most pesticide residue".
arc.evidence: Each claim's verdict, strongest study first.
arc.resolution: Eating organic sharply lowers pesticide residues on your food and in your body, but organic food is not residue-free, and less exposure is not the same as a proven health benefit.
arc.takeaway: A decision rule the viewer can apply.
